strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing genuine challenges in quantizing billion-scale VGGT models through empirical observations of special tokens and multi-view data effects
Strong experimental results: achieving 98% performance retention at W4A4 (88.2 vs 90.0 AUC@30) with substantial margins over state-of-the-art baselines like Quarot
Comprehensive evaluation across multiple benchmarks (Co3Dv2, DTU), metrics, and diverse baseline methods with thorough ablation studies
Thoughtful technical design combining pre-global Hadamard rotation and post-local smoothing with justified ordering; fine-grained quantization granularity well-motivated
Frame-aware clustering cleverly leverages VGGT's inductive bias of first-frame-relative structure for calibration dataset construction
Minimal computational overhead (0.2% latency, 0.02GB memory during calibration) demonstrated through efficiency analysis
Clear presentation with good motivation, informative visualizations, and extensive appendices including formal proofs
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Hadamard rotation from QuaRot (2024), channel-wise scaling from SmoothQuant (2023); main contribution is engineering adaptation to VGGT rather than fundamental algorithmic innovation
Narrow evaluation scope: only VGGT-1B model tested with no evaluation on other 3D reconstruction models (MASt3R, Fast3R) or VGGT variants; limited to 2 datasets

Generalization concerns: frame-aware clustering and special-token analysis are heavily tailored to VGGT's specific architecture; unclear how method would adapt to models without these properties or different inductive biases

Theorem 3.2 provides limited insight beyond standard maximum entropy principle; gap between theory (assuming known domain scales) and practice (K-means clustering approximation) not rigorously analyzed
Hyperparameter sensitivity not addressed: multiple hyperparameters (α=0.5, T=0.2, K=8) lack ablation studies or sensitivity analysis; selection methodology unclear
Hardware deployment specifics unclear: 'real-hardware inference' claims lack details on specific platform (GPU/edge/mobile), affecting reproducibility of speedup and compression results
Missing comparisons: no QAT baseline to establish performance ceiling; no comparison with other compression approaches (pruning, distillation, low-rank factorization)
Limited failure case analysis: paper lacks discussion of when/why method fails, which scene types are challenging, or performance distribution across test samples
Noise score design (Eq. 9) appears ad-hoc; no ablation justifying the specific combination of mean/variance deviations or alternative filtering criteria
Calibration dataset composition uses only Co3Dv2 training data; cross-domain generalization with significantly different distributions not evaluated

strengths: First systematic study of quantization for VGGT, addressing real and well-motivated model-specific challenges (heavy-tailed distributions from special tokens, calibration instability from multi-view data)

Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple datasets (CO3Dv2, DTU, 7-Scenes, NRGBD), tasks, and strong baselines with convincing results (W4A4: 88.2 AUC@30 vs QuaRot 81.6, maintaining 98% of FP performance)
Strong practical impact with 2.5× speedup and 3.7× memory reduction validated on real hardware (RTX 4090) with minimal overhead (0.2% additional latency)
Thorough ablation studies clearly demonstrating contribution of each component (DSFQ, NFDS, fine-grained granularity) with sensitivity analyses showing robustness to hyperparameters
Well-designed frame-aware clustering leveraging VGGT's architectural inductive biases, with clear visualizations motivating the approach
Excellent reproducibility support: detailed experimental settings, hyperparameter studies, code release promised, complete proofs provided
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Hadamard rotation from QuaRot, channel-wise smoothing from SmoothQuant, fine-grained quantization from μ-coherence work; main contribution is their combination for VGGT rather than novel techniques

Theorem 3.2 provides limited conceptual insight—essentially stating 'sample proportionally from clusters' with standard maximum entropy proof; practical frame-aware clustering (Eq. 12) more novel than the theorem itself
Narrow scope: evaluation limited to VGGT and Fast3R (both very recent); frame-aware approach specific to temporal/multi-view architectures, generalization to other models/domains unclear

Insufficient justification for design choices: why cosine similarity of first-frame features optimal? Why 20% outlier filtering threshold (p=0.2)? Why is post-rotation smoothing more stable than pre-rotation? (Table 4 shows difference but lacks intuition)

Marginal calibration efficiency gains: Table 11 shows ~1 point improvement from 5→40 samples; no principled approach for determining calibration budget or deeper analysis of size/performance trade-offs
At W8A8 settings, improvements over QuaRot minimal (89.4 vs 89.4 Table 1); substantial gains concentrated in W4A4 regime, limiting breadth of applicability

Limited architectural generalization: sensitivity to vision backbone (DINOv2), encoder architectures, and scaling behavior unexplored; frame-aware clustering applicability to non-temporal models unclear
Lemma 3.1 on Hadamard central limit effect cited but not rigorously analyzed in VGGT context; 'heavy-tailed distribution' informally defined
